title: Has food inflation lost its bite?
gist: Euro area food inflation fell to 1.1% in August 2026 on past good harvests and lower soft-commodity prices, even as energy pushed headline to 3.8%. The ECB warns a double shock from energy/fertiliser costs (Hormuz blockade) and 2026 heat and drought will lift food inflation to 3.4% by Q3 2027, though the peak should be about one-fifth of 2022's. Food prices remain ~30% above end-2021, keeping affordability and inflation perceptions a monetary policy concern.

themes.theme: Euro area food disinflation amid energy-led headline spike

insights.claim: Euro area headline inflation rose from 1.7% in January 2026 to 3.8% in September 2026, driven mainly by energy commodity prices after the start of the Middle East conflict, with consumer energy inflation at 18.9% in September.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Headline inflation well above target is energy-driven, framing ECB reaction-function debates.
insights.quote: which pushed consumer energy inflation to 18.9% in September
insights.locator: The puzzle of falling food inflation

insights.claim: Euro area food inflation fell from 2.6% in January 2026 to 1.1% in August, its lowest since mid-2021, before edging up to 1.3% in September.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Food disinflation has bottomed; the September uptick may mark a turning point.
insights.quote: its lowest level since mid-2021
insights.locator: The puzzle of falling food inflation

insights.claim: Coffee, chocolate, fruit and dairy, which saw strong price increases in 2025, contributed negligibly to euro area food inflation by September 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Softs-driven food inflation of 2025 has fully washed out of consumer prices.
insights.locator: As for drivers, if we start

insights.claim: Low euro area food inflation mainly reflects earlier favourable factors still feeding through: above-average 2025 European harvests of cereals and oilseeds, lower international prices for coffee, tea, cocoa and sugar, and consequently lower farm-gate prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The tailwinds behind low food inflation are backward-looking and fading.
insights.quote: low food inflation mainly reflects earlier favourable factors that are still feeding through into consumer prices
insights.locator: Next, if we look more deeply

insights.claim: Upstream indicators suggest pipeline pressures on euro area food inflation are building again from a double shock of energy and extreme weather.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Signals a reacceleration in food inflation through 2027.
insights.quote: a double shock from energy and extreme weather could reignite food price pressures
insights.locator: Low food inflation: here to stay?

insights.claim: Energy feeds into food prices largely indirectly via transport, fertilisers, packaging and processing, with effects taking several months to reach consumer prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Lagged pass-through means current energy shock is not yet in food CPI.
insights.quote: These indirect effects can take several months to show up in consumer prices.
insights.locator: Looking first at the energy shock

insights.claim: Fertiliser producer prices have surged since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and unlike in 2022 this reflects direct supply disruption as well as higher energy costs.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Hormuz blockade creates a physical fertiliser supply shock, relevant for agri-input producers and crop costs.
insights.quote: Unlike the situation in 2022, the recent increase in fertiliser prices directly reflects disruption to supply, as well as higher energy costs.
insights.locator: The recent energy shock is having

insights.claim: As of August 2026, later-stage food producer prices in the euro area had not yet increased, reflecting the usual lag in passing through input costs.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The pass-through wave is still ahead, implying upside to food CPI in coming quarters.
insights.locator: The recent energy shock is having

insights.claim: The energy shock will hit energy-intensive farm products hardest: cereals like wheat, maize and barley, downstream bread, pasta and bakery goods, and via animal feed eventually dairy and meat.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Identifies which food categories and processors face the largest cost increases.
insights.quote: A strong impact is expected for products linked to energy-intensive farming.
insights.locator: The energy shock is not expected

insights.claim: Gas prices have risen less than after the pandemic but have increased, especially since summer 2026, raising costs for cereals, oilseeds, vegetables, potatoes and greenhouse heating.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Gas is the key cost channel to watch for fertiliser and greenhouse produce.
insights.quote: Gas prices have risen less than they did in the aftermath of the pandemic.
insights.locator: Gas prices have risen less

insights.claim: Oil shocks reach food prices through transport and indirect costs and can take years to fully pass through, while wholesale gas price changes take even longer to fully reach food prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Long pass-through lags imply food inflation persistence well beyond the energy spike itself.
insights.quote: oil price shocks can take years to fully work their way through to food prices
insights.locator: Oil price increases, by contrast

themes.theme: Extreme weather and El Nino as faster-acting shock

insights.claim: Extremely dry, persistently hot 2026 conditions across large parts of Europe hit crops at a critical stage and will likely push food inflation higher in the coming year.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Weather damage to the 2026 crop supports higher agricultural commodity and food prices.
insights.quote: Heat and drought hit crops at a critical stage of the 2026 season.
insights.locator: Weather is the second factor

insights.claim: ECB staff estimate the 2026 weather shock will add about 0.3-0.8 percentage points to euro area food inflation over the next year, varying by country and product.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Quantifies the weather add-on to food inflation for forecasting.
insights.quote: an effect in the order of 0.3-0.8 percentage points on euro area food inflation over the next year
insights.locator: ECB staff estimates point to

insights.claim: Weather effects show up faster than energy effects because weather acts directly on unprocessed food supply.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Sequencing: weather first in unprocessed food, energy later in processed food, extends the inflation hump.
insights.quote: Weather effects are likely to show up faster than energy effects
insights.locator: Weather effects are likely

insights.claim: September 2026's uptick in euro area food inflation came entirely from unprocessed food, which rose to 4% on weather-sensitive vegetable prices, while processed food slipped to 0.4%.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Processed food at 0.4% has the most room to rise once energy pass-through arrives.
insights.quote: That small uptick from the August data came entirely from unprocessed food inflation, which rose to 4% in September.
insights.locator: In September, these effects

insights.claim: The ongoing El Nino is adding pressure by pushing up food commodity prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Adds a global climate driver to soft commodity upside.
insights.quote: Additional pressures are coming from the ongoing El Niño
insights.locator: So what do we expect

insights.claim: Western Europe was most severely affected by summer 2026 droughts and heatwaves, while the picture in eastern Europe was more mixed.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Regional dispersion implies uneven country-level food inflation.
insights.quote: Western Europe was the region most severely affected by droughts and heatwaves over the summer
insights.locator: When it comes to the impact

themes.theme: Food inflation outlook and model divergence

insights.claim: The September 2026 ECB staff projections see euro area food inflation rising sharply to 3.4% in Q3 2027 before declining.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A near tripling of food inflation into 2027 complicates any easing narrative.
insights.quote: see food inflation rising sharply to reach 3.4% in the third quarter of 2027
insights.locator: So what do we expect

insights.claim: The current energy shock is smaller than 2022's and driven more by oil than gas, so the food inflation peak is expected to be roughly one-fifth of the post-Ukraine-invasion peak.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Argues against a 2022-style food inflation replay, limiting tail-risk.
insights.quote: the peak in food inflation is expected to be roughly one-fifth of that recorded after the start of Russia’s war against Ukraine
insights.locator: The current energy shock is different

insights.claim: Weaker demand than in 2022 may make it harder for firms to pass higher costs into food prices this time.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Margin squeeze risk for food producers and retailers if costs rise but pricing power is weak.
insights.quote: demand is less strong now than in 2022, which means that it may be more difficult to pass higher costs on to food prices
insights.locator: Importantly, demand is less strong

insights.claim: New weather-aware machine-learning models predict a more delayed food inflation response, while other short-term projection models point to an even steeper rise than ECB projections, but all models expect food inflation to increase over 2027.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Direction is consensus across models; timing and magnitude are the uncertainty.
insights.quote: What is, however, common to all models is an expected increase in food inflation over 2027.
insights.locator: In addition, there is still uncertainty

themes.theme: EU fertiliser dependence and policy cushions

insights.claim: Fertilisers account for up to 16% of farmers' input costs, and the EU imports about 30% of its nitrogen-based and 70% of its phosphatic fertilisers, while domestic production is highly gas-dependent.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: EU agriculture is structurally exposed to fertiliser and gas supply shocks.
insights.quote: The EU depends on imports for around 30% of its nitrogen-based fertilisers and 70% of its phosphatic fertilisers
insights.locator: Fertilisers are an important input

insights.claim: In July 2026 the EU approved temporary support covering up to 80% of farmers' additional fertiliser costs plus earlier Common Agricultural Policy direct payments.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Fiscal support may dampen fertiliser cost pass-through and sustain fertiliser demand.
insights.quote: Farmers will receive support covering up to 80% of the additional cost of fertilisers
insights.locator: In July, the EU approved

themes.theme: Food affordability, perceived inflation and policy relevance

insights.claim: The relative price of food versus non-food opened an exceptional and persistent gap between 2022 and 2025; recent low food inflation closed only part of it and ECB projections see it remaining.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Persistent food price level shock keeps inflation perceptions and expectations elevated.
insights.quote: the gap that opened up between 2022 and 2025 was exceptional and persistent
insights.locator: Why the shopping basket still feels expensive

insights.claim: Euro area food prices are about 30% above end-2021 levels, ranging from about 24% in Finland to about 48% in Estonia.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Cross-country dispersion signals uneven affordability and political pressure.
insights.quote: Food prices in the euro area as a whole are around 30% higher than at the end of 2021
insights.locator: Across euro area countries there

insights.claim: Real wages measured against headline inflation are back to pre-surge levels, but wages' purchasing power in terms of food remains below pre-surge levels, especially for frequently bought items.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Consumers' food squeeze persists despite real wage recovery, weighing on sentiment.
insights.quote: wages have recovered but the food shopping basket has become more expensive
insights.locator: Wage dynamics help put inflation

insights.claim: A Eurobarometer survey released 22 September 2026 found 55% of Europeans see reasonable food prices as a top EU priority.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Food affordability is a salient political issue that may drive policy interventions.
insights.quote: 55% of Europeans see reasonable food prices as a top EU priority
insights.locator: This explains why food affordability

insights.claim: Because food is bought frequently it weighs heavily on perceived inflation, so the ECB considers it too early to assume food inflation has lost its bite and sees food prices as relevant for monetary policy.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Signals ECB vigilance on food-driven inflation expectations, a hawkish lean.
insights.quote: It is too early to assume that food inflation has lost its bite.
